newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq puts on dazzling archaeological display.
newsitem.headline: Iraq puts on dazzling archaeological display.

text.p: Iraq's Antiquities Department on Saturday showed a dazzling display of artefacts found by archaeologists over the past six years.
The finds, from across the country, ranged from the lower paleothic periods of about 500,000 years ago to Abbasid times of a little more than 1,000 years from now.

Hand-made implements of stone and obsidian representing scrapers with deeply notched edges came from terraces along the Euphrates and Tigris rivers in northern Iraq, according to Dr Muayad Demeriji, the department's head.
"It is very important to the history of mankind...We did not know we had older than middle-paleothlic," Demeriji said, in reference to a period in Iraq's history which flourished 120,000 years ago.
Demeriji also showed reporters, following a news conference held in the empty rooms of the Iraq Museum, ancient bird sculptures made of river pebbles.
The phallic sculptures, about six of them put in a glass case, had the head of vulture-like birds and came from the site of Nemrik close to the Kurdish province of Dahouk.
"They could have been part of a cult practised in northern Mesopotamia. Maybe we are in front of the earliest forms of religion in this region," said an Iraq Museum expert.

Demeriji said ancient Mesopotamians, who lived between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, had set up some form of agricultural activity relying mainly on crude cultivation of barley and wheat as well as hunting.
"This happened in our land about 10,000 years ago. We have one of the oldest villages in the history of mankind," he said.
On show was a fascinating jar of beautiful motifs of sitting and standing figures discovered in the Abbasid town of Balad close to Mosul which is 400 km (250 miles) north of Baghdad.
Smaller ones, beautifully glazed, came from Kufa, an Islamic city near Najaf 180 km (112 miles) south of Baghdad.
From the stone town of Hatra, which flourished in the second century A.D., were statues of women in tunics and one stone sculpture of an eagle.

In all there were about 200 pieces but they were no match to the 180,000 artefacts originally exhibited in the Iraq Museum but removed and now hidden in packed boxes for fear, in Demeriji's words, of further missile attacks on Baghdad, which was hit by allied planes during the 1991 Gulf War.

Demeriji said lack of vehicles and spare parts was hindering work by his 300 or so archaeologists. He said he had no black-and-white films to document the new discoveries and little digging equipment. Iraq has been under United Nations sanctions for the past six years.
But the scourge of Iraqi antiquities, Demeriji said, was pilfering by illegal diggers and smuggling of precious pieces.
